title: Distribution Water Quality and System Integrity
audience: Practising drinking-water operators and supervisors seeking focused applied development.
prerequisites: Basic operator terminology, metric calculations and access to the source readings. Use a calculator; all supplied facility data are fictional.
introduction: Investigate water age, residual trends, pressure events and repair records using a fictional North Ridge distribution zone. Produce a prioritized monitoring and verification plan.
delivery: Self-paced online pilot: complete 4 modules on your own schedule with case exercises graded automatically, source reading, active-time tracking and a server-graded final assessment. A non-credit pilot learning record is issued automatically after all requirements are met. The seven-hour daily recording limit applies across courses. Breaks and idle periods are excluded. Planned duration requires a timed pilot; no approved CEUs are awarded.

modules.title: Storage turnover and water-age screening
objectives: Calculate a nominal storage turnover indicator.
Explain why an average does not describe the oldest water.
modules.lesson:
### What a turnover indicator actually tells you

A storage turnover indicator is a single quotient: a volume divided by a rate. It answers one narrow question, which is how long the tank would take to pass a volume of water equal to some chosen part of its contents, if the tank behaved like a simple flow-through vessel. It does not measure water age. It does not measure the age of the oldest parcel of water in the tank. It does not tell you whether the tank stratifies, short-circuits between a shared inlet and outlet, or holds a cold dead layer under a warm surface in August.

Treat the number as a screening flag that ranks your storage facilities against each other and against their own history. A reservoir whose indicator moves from roughly three days in winter to roughly nine days in a low-demand shoulder season is telling you that the hydraulic conditions changed, and that residual decay, nitrification in chloraminated systems, disinfection by-product formation and taste and odour complaints are all more likely in that zone. The US EPA Drinking Water Distribution System Tools and Resources material discusses water age, storage and pressure management as interrelated distribution integrity issues. That is United States technical guidance. It is useful for the physics and for investigation structure, and it is not an Ontario requirement. What binds you in Ontario is your Environmental Compliance Approval, your drinking water works permit, your operational plan and the duties and record obligations that flow from O. Reg. 128/04, including sections 23 and 25 to 27 covering designation of overall responsible operator and operator in charge, operator duties and records.

### Defining active volume and the throughput boundary

Most bad turnover numbers come from the two inputs, not from the arithmetic.

Active volume is the volume that actually cycles between the routine low operating level and the routine high operating level. It is not the volume to overflow, and it is not the nameplate capacity on the asset register. Volume below the low operating level is carried continuously and is exactly the water that ages. Volume above the routine high control point is only used during fire flow or upset. If you divide total volume by demand you will overstate the residence time of the water that moves, and if you divide active volume by demand you will understate the residence time of the water that sits. Both numbers are useful. Report both, and label which is which.

Throughput must be the flow that actually exchanges through that tank. Common boundary errors include using a zone master meter that includes a large industrial service teed in upstream of the tank tie-in, using a pumping station total that recirculates through a loop and returns to the same main without passing the tank, and using annual average day demand when you are trying to explain a July problem or an April problem. Choose a representative period that matches the question you are answering, and write down which period you used.

If the tank is a floating reservoir on a single inlet and outlet pipe, recognize that the pipe carries flow in both directions and the tank only exchanges the drawdown and refill volume each cycle. If the tank has a dedicated inlet with an altitude valve and a separate outlet, exchange is generally better but you still need the operating band.

### Worked example 1: nominal turnover on active and total volume

Case assumptions supplied for this example only. Fictional ground reservoir, cylindrical, internal diameter 18.0 m. Recorded routine operating band is 3.2 m to 7.4 m of water depth. Overflow is at 7.6 m. Zone master meter recorded 3,010 m3 over 7 days. A metered bulk customer taps the main upstream of the reservoir tie-in and is recorded at 45 m3/d. These are teaching values, not authorized values.

Step 1, plan area.
Area = 0.7854 x (18.0 m)^2
Area = 0.7854 x 324.0 m2
Area = 254.5 m2

Step 2, active depth.
Active depth = 7.4 m minus 3.2 m
Active depth = 4.2 m

Step 3, active volume.
Active volume = 254.5 m2 x 4.2 m
Active volume = 1,068.9 m3

Step 4, volume at routine high level.
Volume at high level = 254.5 m2 x 7.4 m
Volume at high level = 1,883.3 m3

Step 5, average daily throughput at the meter.
Meter average = 3,010 m3 divided by 7 d
Meter average = 430.0 m3/d

Step 6, correct the boundary.
Exchanging throughput = 430.0 m3/d minus 45 m3/d
Exchanging throughput = 385.0 m3/d

Step 7, nominal turnover on active volume.
Turnover (active) = 1,068.9 m3 divided by 385.0 m3/d
Turnover (active) = 2.78 d

Step 8, nominal turnover on volume held at high level.
Turnover (held) = 1,883.3 m3 divided by 385.0 m3/d
Turnover (held) = 4.89 d

Answer: the nominal active turnover indicator is 2.8 days and the nominal turnover on the full held volume is 4.9 days. If you had used the uncorrected meter total and the full volume you would have reported 1,883.3 m3 divided by 430.0 m3/d, which is 4.38 d, and if you had used active volume with the uncorrected meter you would have reported 2.49 d. The spread between 2.5 d and 4.9 d comes entirely from input definitions.

### Worked example 2: why the average hides the oldest water

Same fictional reservoir. Case assumption: SCADA trends show one fill and draw cycle per day, with the level falling from 7.4 m to 6.1 m overnight before refill.

Step 1, drawdown depth per cycle.
Drawdown = 7.4 m minus 6.1 m
Drawdown = 1.3 m

Step 2, drawdown volume per cycle.
Drawdown volume = 254.5 m2 x 1.3 m
Drawdown volume = 330.9 m3

Step 3, exchange fraction per cycle, referenced to the volume held at high level.
Exchange fraction = 330.9 m3 divided by 1,883.3 m3
Exchange fraction = 0.176, that is 17.6 percent per cycle

Step 4, fraction of original water remaining after n cycles, assuming complete mixing during each cycle.
Remaining fraction = (1 minus 0.176)^n
Remaining fraction = (0.824)^n

Step 5, cycles required to leave 10 percent of the original water.
n = ln(0.10) divided by ln(0.824)
n = (-2.303) divided by (-0.1936)
n = 11.9 cycles

Step 6, convert cycles to days at one cycle per day.
Time to 90 percent replacement = 11.9 cycles x 1.0 d/cycle
Time to 90 percent replacement = 11.9 d

Step 7, cross-check using the continuously stirred tank approximation.
Mean residence time = 1,883.3 m3 divided by 385.0 m3/d = 4.89 d
Time to 90 percent replacement = 2.303 x 4.89 d = 11.3 d

Answer: the nominal active turnover indicator is 2.8 days, the mean residence time is about 4.9 days, and roughly 11 to 12 days are needed before only 10 percent of the original water remains. The oldest 10 percent of the water in that tank is four times older than the headline screening number. That gap is the entire reason an average does not describe the oldest water. If mixing is poor and the tank stratifies, the real tail is worse than either model, because the exchanged volume recirculates near the inlet and the lower or upper dead zone never participates.

### Input register and interpretation matrix

Use a fixed register so two operators calculating the same tank get the same answer.

| Input | Source you must name | Value used | Why it can be wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plan area or volume curve | As-built drawing or calibrated strap chart | 254.5 m2 | Asset register nameplate volume is often the overflow volume |
| Routine low operating level | SCADA setpoint list, current revision | 3.2 m | Seasonal setpoint changes not carried into the calculation |
| Routine high operating level | SCADA setpoint list, current revision | 7.4 m | Altitude valve or control band changed after commissioning |
| Throughput period | Meter totalizer log, dated | 7 d ending on a stated date | Annual average used to explain a seasonal event |
| Upstream or bypass deductions | Zone schematic and customer meter reads | 45 m3/d | Bulk service teed in upstream of the tank tie-in |
| Cycle count per day | SCADA level trend | 1 cycle/d | Multiple partial cycles counted as one |
| Outlet water quality | Sample record with field QC | residual, temperature, turbidity | Sample drawn from the fill line, not the aged volume |

| Screening result | Supporting observation | Reasonable operator response |
|---|---|---|
| Indicator stable, residual stable at tank outlet | No complaints, temperature normal | Record and continue routine monitoring |
| Indicator rising, residual falling at tank outlet | Low-demand season | Increase outlet sampling frequency, trend temperature, raise with the overall responsible operator |
| Indicator stable, residual falling | Possible nitrification or demand in the main | Investigate the main and the tank separately, sample at both |
| Indicator very low, residual falling | Recent main break or repair upstream | Check the disinfection and return to service records for that work |
| Indicator unavailable because inputs conflict | Setpoints and drawings disagree | Do not publish a number, escalate to verify the record |

### Judgment: what changes the answer

Change the operating band and everything moves. Lowering the high control point by one metre in this example removes 254.5 m3 of held volume and shortens the mean residence time, but it also removes emergency and fire storage, changes system pressure and may conflict with the approval for the works. An operator screening exercise never authorizes that change. The correct output is a written review request that states the constraint, the calculated indicator, the supporting observations and the decision owner.

Change the season and the meaning changes. The same 4.9 day mean residence at 4 degrees Celsius and at 22 degrees Celsius are not the same risk, because chlorine decay, nitrification and biofilm activity all accelerate with temperature.

Change the sampling point and the evidence changes. A sample from the inlet or from the tank drain during a fill does not represent the aged water. If you are testing whether the tail is real, draw from the outlet late in a drawdown, and if you are using field turbidity as part of the picture, follow the instrument and laboratory quality control expectations in your procedure. The US EPA Field turbidity measurement material describes field measurement procedure and quality control practice, and it is US technical guidance. Your own sampling plan and the applicable Ontario regulation govern what counts.

If a distribution sample returns an adverse result, the hydraulic screening does not change your reporting duty. In Ontario an immediate verbal report is required, followed by written notice within 24 hours after that report, in accordance with the applicable regulation.

### Common errors

First, dividing overflow volume by annual average day demand and calling the result the water age. This overstates exchange for the moving volume and understates the tail, and it has no defensible basis when the tank rarely reaches overflow.

Second, using a zone master meter without checking the schematic. If a bulk user, a pressure zone feed or a recirculation loop sits on the wrong side of the tank tie-in, the throughput is not exchanging water in that tank. In worked example 1 this single error moved the indicator by about 11 percent, and in systems with a large upstream industrial account it can move it by half.

Third, reporting the nominal indicator as if it were the maximum age. A 2.8 day indicator alongside an 11.9 day time to 90 percent replacement is the same tank. Reporting only the first number will get water quality complaints dismissed that should have been investigated.

Fourth, recalculating after a setpoint change but leaving the old number in the operating record. Records under O. Reg. 128/04 need to show what was done and when. An undated indicator with no named inputs cannot be defended later.

### What to verify before you act

Verify the tank volume curve or strap chart against the as-built drawing, not against the asset spreadsheet. Verify the current low and high control setpoints in the controlling SCADA configuration and note the revision date. Verify the zone schematic to confirm which metered flows actually pass the tank tie-in. Verify the facility Environmental Compliance Approval and drinking water works permit for any constraint on operating levels, storage volume or pressure before proposing an operating band change, and confirm the change path in your operational plan. Verify your sampling plan for the required distribution sampling points and frequencies, and the instrument quality control requirements in your procedure before using field turbidity or residual results as evidence. If the tank has recently been out of service, or if upstream watermain work occurred, verify the return to service records against the applicable edition of the Ontario watermain disinfection procedure, including how that work was classified as planned work, repair or contamination. Confirm the designated overall responsible operator and operator in charge for the subsystem, consistent with O. Reg. 128/04 sections 23 and 25 to 27, and confirm who owns the decision you are recommending.

### Fictional worked scenario

All facilities, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are used for training only. No value here is an authorized setpoint or requirement.

Setting: Township of Marnock, Zone 2 standpipe, fictional. Internal diameter 12.0 m. As-built volume curve confirms a uniform cylinder. SCADA setpoint list, revision dated in the current year, shows a routine operating band of 14.5 m to 19.5 m of water depth. Zone master meter totalizer log shows 2,380 m3 over 7 days. The zone schematic shows a bulk agricultural service teed in upstream of the standpipe tie-in, metered at 85 m3/d.

Records supplied to the learner:
1. SCADA setpoint list, band 14.5 m to 19.5 m, dated.
2. Meter totalizer log, 2,380 m3 over 7 d, dated.
3. Asset spreadsheet listing active volume as 1,131 m3, undated, no source.
4. Maintenance note stating the standpipe is fully turned over every 2.2 days with no stagnation risk, no level data attached.

Records to reject: items 3 and 4. The spreadsheet value of 1,131 m3 corresponds to a 10.0 m band, since 113.1 m2 x 10.0 m equals 1,131 m3, which contradicts the dated 5.0 m operating band. The maintenance note asserts full turnover from a nominal indicator and attaches no drawdown or cycle data, so it cannot support a stagnation conclusion.

Worked solution:
Area = 0.7854 x (12.0 m)^2 = 0.7854 x 144.0 m2 = 113.1 m2
Active depth = 19.5 m minus 14.5 m = 5.0 m
Active volume = 113.1 m2 x 5.0 m = 565.5 m3
Volume at high level = 113.1 m2 x 19.5 m = 2,205.5 m3
Meter average = 2,380 m3 divided by 7 d = 340.0 m3/d
Exchanging throughput = 340.0 m3/d minus 85 m3/d = 255.0 m3/d
Turnover (active) = 565.5 m3 divided by 255.0 m3/d = 2.22 d
Mean residence time = 2,205.5 m3 divided by 255.0 m3/d = 8.65 d
Time to 90 percent replacement = 2.303 x 8.65 d = 19.9 d

Conclusion to record: the 2.2 day figure is a nominal active turnover indicator only. The mean residence time is about 8.7 days and roughly 20 days are needed to replace 90 percent of the stored volume. Escalate to the overall responsible operator with the dated inputs, request outlet residual and temperature trending, and do not alter the operating band without confirming the approval and the decision owner.

Excludes bypass demand from tank throughput.

checks.prompt: A fictional cylindrical ground reservoir has an internal diameter of 15.0 m. Using the plan area method for a nominal turnover calculation, what plan area should be used?
checks.explanation: Plan area is 0.7854 x (15.0 m)^2, which is 176.7 m2. The 706.9 m2 figure comes from wrongly treating the diameter as a radius, and 47.1 m2 is the circumference value, not an area.

checks.prompt: A nominal storage turnover indicator is a single volume divided by a rate. What question does that quotient actually answer for a distribution storage facility?
choices: The measured age of the oldest parcel of water held in the tank
The time to pass a chosen volume if the tank behaved as flow-through
The degree of thermal stratification present in the tank in August
The confirmed disinfection by-product formation potential in the zone
checks.explanation: The indicator only estimates how long it would take to pass a chosen volume in an idealized flow-through vessel, so it is a screening flag. It does not measure the oldest parcel, stratification or by-product formation, which is why the oldest water answer is wrong.

checks.prompt: In a turnover screening calculation, which volume is described as active volume?
choices: The nameplate capacity listed on the asset register record
The volume between the low level and the overflow elevation
The volume that cycles between routine low and high levels
The volume carried below the routine low operating level
checks.explanation: Active volume is the band that actually cycles between routine low and routine high operating levels. Nameplate or to-overflow volumes include water that is only used in fire flow or upset, so they overstate the residence time of moving water.

checks.prompt: A zone master meter reads 4,200 m3 over 7 days, but a metered bulk customer taking 60 m3/d is teed into the main upstream of the tank tie-in. What throughput should be used for that tank?
choices: 60 m3/d, using only the metered bulk customer consumption
600 m3/d, since the master meter total is the zone record
660 m3/d, adding the bulk service to the meter average
540 m3/d, deducting flow that never exchanges through the tank
checks.explanation: The meter average is 600 m3/d, and the 60 m3/d bulk service never passes the tank, so exchanging throughput is 540 m3/d. Using the uncorrected 600 m3/d overstates exchange and shortens the reported turnover indicator.

checks.prompt: United States EPA distribution system tools and resources material discusses water age, storage and pressure management together. How should an Ontario operator treat that material?
choices: As useful technical guidance that is not an Ontario requirement
As a replacement for the operational plan sampling provisions
As the governing document for drinking water works permits
As enforceable Ontario limits for storage facility water age
checks.explanation: The US material is helpful for the physics and investigation structure but carries no Ontario legal force. Ontario duties come from the Environmental Compliance Approval, drinking water works permit, operational plan and O. Reg. 128/04, so calling it enforceable is wrong.

checks.prompt: An operator finds that the SCADA setpoint list and the as-built volume curve disagree about the routine high operating level of a reservoir. What is the appropriate next step for the turnover screening?
choices: Substitute nameplate volume until the drawings are reissued
Withhold the number and escalate to verify the record first
Publish the number using the higher of the two level records
Average the two records and note the uncertainty in the log
checks.explanation: When inputs conflict, publishing any figure creates a false record that other operators will reuse, so the value should be withheld and the record verified. Averaging or using the higher level simply hides the conflict inside a number that looks defensible.

modules.title: Spatial residual patterns and investigation design
objectives: Compare matched locations and operating periods.
Distinguish a pattern from proof of its cause.
modules.lesson:
### What a residual reading is evidence of

A chlorine residual reading is a measurement of one water parcel, at one tap, at one instant, by one method, on one instrument. It is not a property of the pipe, the zone or the neighbourhood. Everything you later claim about the distribution system is an inference built on top of that single parcel, and the inference is only as strong as the conditions you documented around it.

That matters because residual investigations almost always begin with a pattern: three low results in the same subdivision, a downward drift at one distal station, a difference between the north and south sides of a pressure zone. A pattern is a reason to investigate. It is not proof of a mechanism. The same spatial pattern of declining free chlorine can be produced by long detention time in an under-turned reservoir, by a dead-end with almost no demand, by nitrification in a chloraminated zone, by a private-side plumbing issue at the sample tap, by a closed or partly closed valve that has redirected flow, by a source or blend change upstream, by biofilm and corroded unlined cast iron exerting wall demand, or by an analytical error such as an expired reagent or an uncleaned sample cell. Several of these can be true at once.

The operator's job in this module is narrow and demanding: build a comparison that can actually separate those explanations, and be honest in writing about what the comparison can and cannot support. The US EPA resource Drinking Water Distribution System Tools and Resources is useful background on water age, storage turnover and pressure management as drivers of distribution water quality, but it is United States technical guidance. It does not set Ontario requirements. Your residual expectations, sampling locations, frequencies and response actions come from the applicable Ontario regulation, your system's Drinking Water Works Permit and Municipal Drinking Water Licence, your Environmental Compliance Approval where applicable, and your documented operational procedures.

### Matching: the four things that must line up

A comparison is matched when the only meaningful thing that differs between the two data sets is the factor you are testing. In distribution work, four dimensions have to line up before a difference means anything.

Location matching. Compare a distal dead-end to another distal dead-end of similar pipe material, diameter, length and service density, not to a sample station on a transmission main. Compare the same tap, same fixture, same flush protocol.

Operating period matching. Sample under a documented operating state: which source or blend is in service, reservoir level and direction of travel, booster pump status, pressure reducing valve setpoints, any valve that is out of its normal position, hydrant flushing or construction in the area, and demand condition. Two samples taken at 09:00 on different days are not matched if one day the reservoir was filling and the other day it was draining.

Analyte and method matching. Free chlorine and total chlorine are different measurements. Combined chlorine is total minus free. A grab sample analysed by a field colorimeter and a continuous analyser reading are different data streams with different drift and different response times. Field turbidity has its own quality control requirements, and the US EPA field turbidity measurement guidance describes the field procedure and quality control elements such as cell cleanliness, condensation, indexed cells and verification standards. Your local laboratory and site methods govern which method is acceptable for your records.

Record matching. Every field record must be attributable. O. Reg. 128/04 addresses operator designation, operator duties and records, including the requirement that operators record what they did and what they observed. A residual investigation that cannot name the operator, the instrument and the time is not evidence.

Use a single register so the matching fields are collected every time rather than reconstructed afterwards.

| Field | Entry | Why it is needed |
|---|---|---|
| Site ID and tap type | e.g. DS-14, dedicated sample station | Fixes location comparability |
| Date and clock time | 24 h local | Pairs sample to operating state |
| Flush time and flow | minutes, approximate L/min | Removes premise or riser water |
| Free Cl2 (mg/L) | to 0.01 mg/L | Primary analyte |
| Total Cl2 (mg/L) | to 0.01 mg/L | Enables combined chlorine check |
| Method and instrument ID | DPD colorimeter serial | Traceability and drift review |
| Reagent lot and expiry | lot number, date | Common invalidation cause |
| Verification check result | standard or blank result | Shows instrument was fit for use |
| Water temperature | degrees C | Affects decay and nitrification risk |
| Turbidity (NTU) and method | field or lab | Supports disturbance hypotheses |
| Operating state | source, blend, tank level and direction, pumps, valves, flushing | The matching variable |
| Operator name and licence | printed and signed | Record duty under O. Reg. 128/04 |
| Comments | odour, colour, works nearby | Context that dies if unwritten |

### Worked example 1: matched pair and difference in differences

All values below are supplied case assumptions for teaching. They are not authorized values for any real system.

Site A is a distal dead-end sample station. Site M is a matched distal dead-end of similar pipe material and length on the same pressure zone, used as a control. Both are sampled with the same colorimeter, same reagent lot, same flush protocol.

Step 1. Baseline free chlorine at Site A, six readings collected over three weeks under the documented normal operating state:
0.84 mg/L + 0.80 mg/L + 0.83 mg/L + 0.79 mg/L + 0.85 mg/L + 0.81 mg/L = 4.92 mg/L
4.92 mg/L / 6 = 0.82 mg/L

Step 2. Current free chlorine at Site A, three readings in one week under the same documented operating state:
0.52 mg/L + 0.50 mg/L + 0.51 mg/L = 1.53 mg/L
1.53 mg/L / 3 = 0.51 mg/L

Step 3. Absolute change at Site A:
0.82 mg/L - 0.51 mg/L = 0.31 mg/L decrease

Step 4. Relative change at Site A, stated against the baseline:
0.31 mg/L / 0.82 mg/L x 100 = 37.8 percent decrease

Step 5. The control site over the same two periods:
baseline mean = 0.79 mg/L, current mean = 0.76 mg/L
0.79 mg/L - 0.76 mg/L = 0.03 mg/L decrease

Step 6. Difference in differences, which is the number that isolates Site A from a system-wide shift:
0.31 mg/L - 0.03 mg/L = 0.28 mg/L

Step 7. Is 0.28 mg/L bigger than the measurement noise? Assume a supplied expanded uncertainty of plus or minus 0.03 mg/L on each mean. For a comparison built from four means:
square root of (4 x (0.03 mg/L)^2) = square root of (0.0036 (mg/L)^2) = 0.06 mg/L
0.28 mg/L / 0.06 mg/L = 4.7 times the combined uncertainty

Step 8. Free versus total, same sampling events:
baseline: total 0.88 mg/L - free 0.82 mg/L = combined 0.06 mg/L
current: total 0.69 mg/L - free 0.51 mg/L = combined 0.18 mg/L
free as a fraction of total, baseline: 0.82 / 0.88 x 100 = 93.2 percent
free as a fraction of total, current: 0.51 / 0.69 x 100 = 73.9 percent

Answer. Site A shows a 0.31 mg/L decrease, 37.8 percent of its own baseline, and 0.28 mg/L of that change is specific to Site A rather than shared with the matched control. The change is roughly 4.7 times the combined measurement uncertainty, so it is unlikely to be instrument noise. The combined chlorine tripled from 0.06 mg/L to 0.18 mg/L, which points toward increased demand or ammonia-related reactions at that location rather than a simple dilution. That is a localized, measurable, real pattern. It is still not a cause.

### Worked example 2: travel time sets the sampling window

Suppose the feed to Site A is a single 150 mm main, 1,850 m long, from a known junction. Supplied case values.

Step 1. Cross-sectional area:
A = 3.1416 / 4 x (0.150 m)^2 = 0.7854 x 0.0225 m^2 = 0.01767 m^2

Step 2. Segment volume:
V = 0.01767 m^2 x 1,850 m = 32.69 m^3

Step 3. Daytime flow of 4.2 L/s converted:
4.2 L/s / 1,000 L/m^3 = 0.0042 m^3/s

Step 4. Daytime travel time:
t = 32.69 m^3 / 0.0042 m^3/s = 7,783 s
7,783 s / 3,600 s/h = 2.16 h

Step 5. Night flow of 0.9 L/s:
0.9 L/s / 1,000 L/m^3 = 0.0009 m^3/s
t = 32.69 m^3 / 0.0009 m^3/s = 36,322 s
36,322 s / 3,600 s/h = 10.09 h

Step 6. Ratio of the two travel times:
10.09 h / 2.16 h = 4.67 times longer at night

Step 7. Descriptive first-order decay using the daytime travel time, junction residual 0.82 mg/L and Site A residual 0.51 mg/L:
ln(0.82 mg/L / 0.51 mg/L) = ln(1.608) = 0.475
k = 0.475 / 2.16 h = 0.220 per hour

Step 8. The same two residuals using the night travel time:
k = 0.475 / 10.09 h = 0.047 per hour

Answer. Travel time in this segment ranges from about 2.16 h to about 10.09 h depending on demand, so a downstream grab taken at the same clock time as the upstream grab is not sampling the same water. The paired downstream sample must be offset by the travel time applicable to that operating period. The decay coefficient derived from the same two residuals differs by a factor of 4.7 depending only on the hydraulic assumption. Report the coefficient as a descriptive estimate with its assumptions stated, never as a measured system property, and never as a disinfection credit. Plug flow with no blending, no storage contribution and steady demand are idealisations that rarely hold in a looped network.

### Designing the next round to discriminate hypotheses

A sampling round that cannot change your mind is a waste of reagent. Before you write the plan, state for each hypothesis what result would support it and what result would kill it.

| Hypothesis | Discriminating observation | Main confounder | Next action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long detention in the zone | Residual improves after documented turnover increase, control site unchanged | Turnover change coincides with a source change | Sample under two documented turnover states, same source |
| Local sample tap or premise issue | Residual normal at the nearest hydrant or adjacent service, low only at that tap | Hydrant flush changes local hydraulics | Sample tap, adjacent service and hydrant in one round |
| Valve out of normal position | Pressure or flow pattern inconsistent with records, residual boundary follows a hydraulic line | Recent flushing programme | Field valve verification, compare to valve records |
| Nitrification in chloraminated zone | Rising combined chlorine loss, nitrite trend, temperature elevated | Analytical interference | Add nitrite and ammonia to the round, check temperature record |
| Upstream source or blend change | Change appears at the zone inlet and at the control site as well | Simultaneous demand shift | Compare inlet, control and suspect site in the same window |
| Analytical error | Difference disappears on a second instrument, or verification standard fails | Two instruments share a bad reagent lot | Duplicate with second verified instrument and fresh lot |
| Recent repair or new main | Pattern starts at a work site date, turbidity elevated | Seasonal demand shift | Review disinfection and commissioning records for that work |

Where recent watermain work is in scope, the Ontario watermain disinfection procedure is the reference for planned work, repairs and the classification of contamination, and you must use the current applicable edition. If your investigation touches a repair or a new main, pull the disinfection, flushing, sampling and return to service records for that work before you theorize.

One more design rule. Decide the response before you see the result. If a confirmatory round returns a residual below what the applicable regulation and your approval require, you are no longer in an investigation, you are in a response with defined notification steps. In Ontario, an adverse drinking water test result requires an immediate verbal report to the specified parties, followed by written notice within 24 hours after that verbal report. Know that path before you send anyone into the field.

### Common errors

Comparing free chlorine to total chlorine across periods. An operator sees 0.82 mg/L last month and 0.69 mg/L today and reports a decline, without noticing that last month's value was free and today's was total. The apparent decline is smaller than reality, because free dropped from 0.82 mg/L to 0.51 mg/L. Any total reading lower than the free reading from the same sample is physically impossible and invalidates the record.

Calling a route a profile. Samples collected along a main over three hours in a truck are not a snapshot. Demand, tank level and source blend all moved during the route, and the water at the last site left the junction hours before the first sample was drawn. Presenting them as a single instantaneous gradient overstates the spatial trend and hides the temporal one.

Dropping the control site once the suspect site looks interesting. Without the matched control, you cannot tell a site-specific problem from a zone-wide or plant-side shift. Example 1 collapses entirely if the control data are missing, because the whole 0.31 mg/L could have been system-wide.

Inconsistent flushing at the tap. Thirty seconds one day and five minutes the next changes what you are measuring from premise and riser water to main water. Record the flush time every time and keep it constant.

Treating a fitted decay coefficient as a measured fact. As shown in example 2, the same residual pair yields 0.220 per hour or 0.047 per hour depending purely on the assumed travel time. Publishing one figure without the hydraulic assumption misleads everyone downstream of the report.

### What to verify before you act

Verify your system's Drinking Water Works Permit, Municipal Drinking Water Licence and any applicable Environmental Compliance Approval for the sampling locations, residual expectations and operational requirements that apply to your system specifically. Do not import a number from a textbook, a neighbouring utility or United States guidance.

Verify the applicable Ontario regulation for sampling, analysis and reporting, including the notification path for an adverse result, and confirm the current version rather than a printout in a binder.

Verify operator designation, duties and record requirements under O. Reg. 128/04, sections 23 and 25 to 27, so that the people collecting and interpreting the data are authorized to do so and the records satisfy the duty to record.

Verify the current applicable edition of the Ontario watermain disinfection procedure if any part of the pattern coincides with planned work, a repair, or a suspected contamination event, and read the classification guidance before deciding what the work means for your zone.

Verify the instrument record: last verification, reagent lot and expiry, cell condition, and whether the same instrument produced both the baseline and the current data. Verify the field turbidity procedure and its quality control steps against your local method, using the US EPA field turbidity measurement guidance only as technical background.

Verify the operating record: SCADA trends for reservoir level, source in service, booster pump run times, pressure, and any valve, flushing or construction activity in the window. If the operating record and the field log disagree, resolve the conflict in writing before you draw a conclusion. Retain the field register, instrument verification records, SCADA extracts, valve and work orders, and the written rationale for each hypothesis you kept and each one you rejected. That retained set, not the conclusion, is what defends the decision later.

### Fictional worked scenario

All facilities, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are used only for training. No value here is an authorized limit or setpoint.

Harbourview Distribution System, Zone 3. Two matched distal dead-ends, DE-7 and DE-9, similar diameter, material and service density, both sampled at dedicated stations with a five minute flush.

Supplied records:

| Record | Site | Date and time | Free Cl2 mg/L | Total Cl2 mg/L | Instrument ID |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | DE-7 | Tue 09:30 | 0.74 | 0.79 | CL-102 |
| 2 | DE-9 | Tue 09:55 | 0.71 | 0.77 | CL-102 |
| 3 | DE-7 | Thu 09:35 | 0.38 | 0.30 | CL-102 |
| 4 | DE-9 | Thu 10:00 | 0.66 | 0.72 | CL-102 |
| 5 | DE-7 | Thu 09:40 | 0.70 | not recorded | blank |

DE-7 is fed by 1,200 m of 200 mm main from the Zone 3 inlet. Thursday daytime flow in that main is 2.5 L/s.

Records you must reject. Record 5 has no instrument ID, and the instrument log shows CL-102 was out for verification from 08:00 to 11:15 Thursday, so nothing at DE-7 on Thursday morning could have come from a verified unit other than the entries already attributed. An unattributed 0.70 mg/L that contradicts a verified 0.38 mg/L cannot be used. Record 3 also fails an internal check: total chlorine must be equal to or greater than free chlorine.
0.30 mg/L - 0.38 mg/L = -0.08 mg/L combined, which is impossible.
The free value may still be usable, but the total is void and must be reflagged and recollected.

Matched comparison using the verified free values:
Tuesday difference between sites: 0.74 mg/L - 0.71 mg/L = 0.03 mg/L
Thursday difference between sites: 0.66 mg/L - 0.38 mg/L = 0.28 mg/L
Change in the site-to-site difference: 0.28 mg/L - 0.03 mg/L = 0.25 mg/L
DE-9 own change: 0.71 mg/L - 0.66 mg/L = 0.05 mg/L, which is 7.0 percent of 0.71 mg/L
DE-7 own change: 0.74 mg/L - 0.38 mg/L = 0.36 mg/L, which is 48.6 percent of 0.74 mg/L

Travel time to DE-7 for the paired upstream sample:
A = 0.7854 x (0.200 m)^2 = 0.03142 m^2
V = 0.03142 m^2 x 1,200 m = 37.70 m^3
Q = 2.5 L/s / 1,000 L/m^3 = 0.0025 m^3/s
t = 37.70 m^3 / 0.0025 m^3/s = 15,080 s = 4.19 h

Conclusion. The loss is specific to DE-7, not zone wide. The next round pairs a Zone 3 inlet sample with a DE-7 sample offset by about 4.2 h, adds the adjacent hydrant and one service, recollects total chlorine on a verified instrument, and pulls valve and repair records for the DE-7 branch. The pattern is real. The cause is not yet established.

modules.title: Pressure events and repair verification
objectives: Identify the records needed to apply the current repair procedure.
modules.lesson:
### What a pressure reading proves and what it cannot

A pressure logger tells you the pressure at one gauge, at one elevation, at the instants it sampled. It does not tell you the pressure at the top of the zone, at the customer service on the hill, or at the repair excavation itself. When you reconstruct an integrity event, you are building an inference from sparse point data toward a statement about a volume of pipe. Every step in that inference either holds up on the record or it does not.

Three separate questions get confused in the field. First, was hydraulic margin lost, and where. Second, was the pipe interior exposed to a contamination pathway, which is a physical and observational question rather than a pressure question. Third, has the work been verified and authorized for return to service under the applicable procedure. A restored pressure trace answers only part of the first question. It is not evidence about the second or third. The Ontario watermain disinfection procedure, current applicable edition, is the document that sorts repair and contamination conditions into classifications and sets out what each classification requires. Your facility's authorized operating procedures and its approval sit on top of that. Nothing in this module authorizes a clearance decision.

The US EPA resource Drinking Water Distribution System Tools and Resources is useful background on pressure management, water age and integrity concepts, and it is United States technical guidance. It is not an Ontario requirement and should never be quoted as one in your event file.

### Timeline reconstruction: clocks, intervals and event order

An integrity-event timeline is a defensible ordering of discrete events with a stated uncertainty for each. The events that must be kept separate are: pressure excursion observed, cause identified, isolation achieved, excavation exposed, break or cut condition observed, repair physically complete, disinfection step performed, flushing performed, sample collected, laboratory result received, and authorization to return to service given. Collapsing any two of these is the most common failure in an event reconstruction. "Sample collected" is not "result received." "Result received" is not "authorized to return to service." A result pending is not a satisfactory result.

Three data-quality problems recur.

Clock offset. Loggers, SCADA historians, laptop-generated repair logs and cell-phone photographs each carry their own clock. If the logger clock is fast, corrected timestamps move earlier, and the apparent order of the excursion relative to a valve closure can reverse. Record the offset you measured, the reference clock you used, and the direction of the correction.

Sampling interval. A logger on a five minute interval cannot resolve a two minute transient and cannot prove one did not occur. The interval sets a floor on your resolution and it also sets the uncertainty band on any duration you report.

Missing data. A gap is not a period of normal pressure. If the logger was not deployed, was in fault, or the memory wrapped, the honest entry is "no data" and the affected interval is unresolved.

O. Reg. 128/04, in the portions dealing with designation, operator duties and records, is the reason your entries matter beyond the incident file. Records made by operators are the evidence that duties were carried out, and an unsigned or undated entry weakens that evidence even if the work was done correctly.

### Worked example 1: elevation-corrected pressure at the critical node

All values below are supplied case assumptions for this teaching example at a fictional facility. They are not authorized values.

Supplied: logger L-7 is on a hydrant port, gauge datum elevation 148.30 m. Its lowest recorded sample during the event is 312 kPa. The critical service in the affected area is at elevation 163.85 m and lies 420 m of 150 mm main downstream of the logger. A model run supplied for the event gives a hydraulic gradient of 4.2 m per 1000 m at the flows present. Unit weight of water is taken as 9.804 kPa per metre of head.

Step 1. Elevation difference.
163.85 m minus 148.30 m = 15.55 m of elevation rise.

Step 2. Convert elevation rise to pressure loss.
15.55 m x 9.804 kPa/m = 152.4 kPa.

Step 3. Friction loss over 420 m.
420 m x 4.2 m per 1000 m = 420 m x 0.0042 m/m = 1.764 m of head.
1.764 m x 9.804 kPa/m = 17.3 kPa.

Step 4. Estimated pressure at the critical service.
312 kPa minus 152.4 kPa minus 17.3 kPa = 142.3 kPa.
Expressed as head: 142.3 kPa divided by 9.804 kPa/m = 14.5 m of head.

Step 5. Apply instrument and datum uncertainty.
Gauge accuracy supplied as plus or minus 0.25 percent of a 1000 kPa span: 0.0025 x 1000 kPa = 2.5 kPa.
Survey datum uncertainty supplied as plus or minus 0.15 m: 0.15 m x 9.804 kPa/m = 1.5 kPa.
Worst case low: 142.3 kPa minus 2.5 kPa minus 1.5 kPa = 138.3 kPa.

Answer: the estimated minimum pressure at the critical service during the recorded event is about 142 kPa, with a defensible lower bound near 138 kPa, or roughly 14.1 to 14.5 m of head. Report the range, the datum, and the gradient source. Reporting "312 kPa, no issue" would be wrong by more than 170 kPa at the point that matters.

### Worked example 2: bounding the excursion, then sizing the flush

Supplied case values, fictional. Logger interval 300 s. Corrected for a verified logger clock offset of 3 min 20 s fast, the samples read: 02:06:40 at 265 kPa, 02:11:40 at 41 kPa, 02:16:40 at 33 kPa, 02:21:40 at 58 kPa, 02:26:40 at 214 kPa. The facility procedure for this example uses a review trigger of 140 kPa at the node.

Step 1. Count samples below the trigger.
Samples below 140 kPa: 3 samples.

Step 2. Measured duration between first and last low sample.
02:21:40 minus 02:11:40 = 10 min. This is the lower bound, because the excursion may have begun just before the first low sample and ended just after the last.

Step 3. Upper bound from interval geometry.
The excursion cannot have started before the last normal sample or ended after the next normal sample.
02:26:40 minus 02:06:40 = 20 min. Upper bound is 20 min.
Equivalently, (3 samples minus 1) x 5 min = 10 min lower bound, and (3 samples plus 1) x 5 min = 20 min upper bound.

Step 4. State the result honestly.
Answer: the low-pressure interval was between 10 and 20 minutes, centred near 15 minutes. The single figure 15 min is a point estimate, not a maximum.

Step 5. Volume of the isolated section for flushing.
Supplied: 268 m of 150 mm main and 42 m of 200 mm main between closed valves.
Area 150 mm: (pi divided by 4) x (0.150 m)^2 = 0.01767 m2.
Volume: 0.01767 m2 x 268 m = 4.736 m3 = 4736 L.
Area 200 mm: (pi divided by 4) x (0.200 m)^2 = 0.03142 m2.
Volume: 0.03142 m2 x 42 m = 1.319 m3 = 1319 L.
Total: 4736 L plus 1319 L = 6055 L = 6.055 m3.

Step 6. Flush duration at the measured discharge.
Supplied hydrant discharge 22 L/s.
One section volume: 6055 L divided by 22 L/s = 275 s = 4.6 min.
Three section volumes, as assumed by the facility procedure in this example: 3 x 4.6 min = 13.8 min, say 14 min.
Water used: 3 x 6.055 m3 = 18.2 m3.

Step 7. Check scouring velocity in the smaller pipe.
22 L/s = 0.022 m3/s.
0.022 m3/s divided by 0.01767 m2 = 1.24 m/s.

Answer: about 14 minutes and 18.2 m3 to move three section volumes, at roughly 1.24 m/s in the 150 mm main. Volume turnover is a planning number only. Clearance depends on the requirements of the current Ontario watermain disinfection procedure for the applicable repair or contamination classification, including any disinfection, stabilisation and sampling steps, plus your own approval and procedures. Field turbidity used to judge stabilisation must follow the method and quality-control practice your laboratory or site method requires; the US EPA field turbidity measurement guidance describes calibration verification, cell handling, bubble exclusion and blank checks that make a field reading usable at all.

### The record register for applying the current repair procedure

Build this register before you attempt to classify the event, not after. If a row is blank, the classification rests on an assumption and you must say so in writing.

| Record | Custodian or source | What it establishes | What invalidates or weakens it | Timeline field it fills |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pressure logger export, raw | Logger download, unedited file | Point pressure, interval, gaps | Edited file, no clock check, wrapped memory | Excursion start and end bounds |
| SCADA trend for zone inlet and tower level | Historian | Zone-wide behaviour, refill timing | Tag out of calibration, poll rate coarser than event | Cause and recovery |
| Gauge or logger calibration record | Instrument file | Usable accuracy band | Expired verification, no serial number match | Uncertainty on every pressure figure |
| Valve operation log | Operating staff | Isolation achieved and released | Times estimated after the fact, no operator name | Isolation and de-isolation |
| Excavation and condition observations, with photographs | Crew and supervisor | Pathway exposure, submergence, sewage proximity, pipe condition | Photos with no timestamp, condition described only verbally | Contamination classification inputs |
| Repair work record | Crew lead | Materials, fittings, method, completion time | Unsigned, undated, no materials listed | Repair complete |
| Disinfection and flushing record | Operator performing work | Steps actually performed, volumes, discharge point | Volumes back-calculated from an assumed hydrant flow | Disinfection and flushing steps |
| Field chlorine residual and turbidity readings | Operator, with QC log | Stabilisation trend at the sampling point | Meter not verified, no blank or standard check, no sample point identified | Stabilisation before sampling |
| Sample collection record and chain of custody | Sampler and laboratory | Time, point, sampler, preservation | Missing collection time, wrong bottle, no custody signature | Sample collected |
| Laboratory report, licensed laboratory | Laboratory | Result and method | Verbal result with no written report to follow, wrong sample point | Result received |
| Authorization to return to service | Overall responsible operator or designate per facility procedure | Who decided, on what basis, when | Decision recorded before the governing results existed | Return to service |
| Notification log | Operator in charge | Who was told, when, what was said | Message content not recorded | Communications |

Retain the raw logger file, not just the graph you pasted into a report. Retain the calibration records that bracket the event date. Retain the field QC log for any meter whose reading you relied on. Under O. Reg. 128/04, in the portions on operator designation, duties and records, the identity and designation of the person who made each decision matter as much as the decision itself.

### When a condition changes, the decision changes

A pressure event with no excavation, no dewatering and no open pipe is a different problem from a break repair in a wet trench beside a sanitary sewer. The classification in the current Ontario watermain disinfection procedure drives the required response, and the inputs to that classification come from observation at the excavation, not from the pressure trace. Common condition changes that alter what you must do include: whether the main was fully depressurized or held a positive pressure throughout, whether the trench was dewatered before the pipe was opened, whether the interior was submerged or contacted soil or sewage, whether the repair was a clamp on an unopened pipe or a cut-in of new pipe and fittings, whether a cross connection or backflow pathway existed on an affected service, and whether the affected area includes a hospital, food plant or other high-consequence customer.

Water quality signals shift the picture as well. Loss of residual at a downstream monitoring point, a turbidity rise that does not clear with continued flushing, or customer complaints of odour or discolouration in an unexpected area all widen the affected zone beyond the isolated section. If a drinking water test result is adverse, Ontario requires an immediate verbal report to the parties named in the applicable regulation, followed by written notice within 24 hours after that verbal report. Do not wait for a second confirming sample before making the verbal report.

If you cannot bound the excursion because data are missing, treat the unresolved interval as unresolved and escalate under your procedure. Manufacturing a number to close a box is worse than an honest gap.

### Common errors

Using the logger reading as the system minimum. The logger sits where it was convenient, usually low in the zone. Elevation alone moved the figure by 152 kPa in Worked example 1. Any statement about minimum pressure in the affected area must be elevation corrected and must name the datum used.

Reporting a point duration as a maximum. Counting three low samples on a five minute logger and writing "15 minute excursion" understates the possible duration by a third. The defensible statement is a bounded range with the logging interval stated.

Treating a data gap as a pass. A logger in fault, a wrapped memory or a SCADA tag outage produces no evidence of normal pressure. Writing "no low pressure recorded" when nothing was recorded at all is a false statement in the event file.

Collapsing sampling and authorization. Signing a return to service at the time the sample was collected, with the laboratory report arriving later, creates a record that cannot be defended. Also avoid announcing "all clear" to customers or to management on the strength of restored pressure while integrity and water quality verification is still open.

Back-calculating flush volumes from an assumed hydrant flow. If the discharge was never measured, the flush volume in your record is an estimate and must be labelled as one. A diffuser with no flow measurement gives you a duration, not a volume.

### What to verify before you act

Consult, in this order: your facility's Environmental Compliance Approval or drinking water works permit and the operational plan procedures issued under your quality management system; the current applicable edition of the Ontario watermain disinfection procedure for the repair and contamination classification that fits what the crew actually observed; and O. Reg. 128/04 in the portions covering operator designation, duties and records, to confirm who may make and record the decision you are about to make. Verify that the person authorizing return to service holds the designation your procedure requires, that the sampling plan and sample points you are using are the ones named in the approved documents, and that every instrument whose reading you are relying on has a current verification record. Confirm the laboratory is licensed for the parameters requested and that you have written results in hand, not a verbal indication. If any of those checks fails, the correct action is to keep the section isolated or under restriction and escalate, not to proceed and document afterward.

### Fictional worked scenario: Maplecrest Water System, event file IE-2026-014

All facilities, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are supplied only for this teaching exercise. No value here is an authorized setpoint or requirement.

Supplied records. A 200 mm main break was reported on Kildare Road. Logger LG-3 sits on a hydrant at datum elevation 152.40 m. Corrected for a verified clock offset of 2 min 10 s slow, LG-3 recorded at a 300 s interval: 03:12:10 at 341 kPa, 03:17:10 at 62 kPa, 03:22:10 at 48 kPa, 03:27:10 at 288 kPa. The highest service in the affected area is at elevation 168.05 m, and the supplied model gradient for the event is 3.6 m per 1000 m over 300 m of main. Crew log entries: "valves closed 03:31", "pipe cut and sleeve installed, trench held about 300 mm of water, pipe interior submerged, 05:40", "flushed, 06:10", "samples taken 06:20", "system returned to service 06:25, all clear". A separate typed summary states "minimum pressure 341 kPa, no low pressure event, no contamination pathway." The laboratory report for the 06:20 samples is dated the following afternoon. The flushing record shows 12 minutes of hydrant discharge with no flow measurement.

Record the learner must reject. The typed summary. It contradicts the raw logger file, which shows two samples below 70 kPa, and it contradicts the crew observation of a submerged open pipe interior. It also conflicts with the return to service entry, which precedes the laboratory report by roughly one day. The 12 minute flush cannot be converted to a volume because no discharge was measured.

Worked solution.

Elevation difference: 168.05 m minus 152.40 m = 15.65 m.
15.65 m x 9.804 kPa/m = 153.4 kPa.
Friction: 300 m x 0.0036 m/m = 1.08 m; 1.08 m x 9.804 kPa/m = 10.6 kPa.
Node pressure at the 48 kPa sample: 48 kPa minus 153.4 kPa minus 10.6 kPa = minus 116 kPa, that is, no pressure and negative head potential at that elevation.

Excursion bounds: low samples 2.
Lower bound (2 minus 1) x 5 min = 5 min.
Upper bound (2 plus 1) x 5 min = 15 min.

Defensible findings: an unresolved excursion of 5 to 15 minutes with zero pressure at the high service, an observed submerged open pipe interior, an unquantified flush, and an authorization recorded before results existed. The classification and required response must be taken from the current Ontario watermain disinfection procedure and the facility procedures, not from the "all clear" entry.

The excavation observation needs classification by the responsible team using applicable procedure evidence. Mechanical completion does not establish water-quality clearance. Require the actual flushing verification, analytical status and authorized return decision. checks.prompt: A pressure logger on a hydrant port records a minimum of 285 kPa during an integrity event. What does that single figure actually establish?
choices: Pressure at that gauge datum at the instants it sampled
Minimum pressure anywhere in the affected pressure zone
Pressure inside the open repair excavation at that time
Proof that no shorter transient occurred between samples
checks.explanation: A logger reports point pressure at one elevation at discrete sample instants. It says nothing about the top of the zone or the excavation, and it cannot prove that no transient occurred between samples, so the zone-wide reading choice is a common overreach.

checks.prompt: A logger set to a 300 s interval covers an event in which a suspected 2 minute transient occurred. What can the record support?
choices: It proves that no transient occurred, since no low sample was recorded
It cannot resolve the transient, and cannot prove one did not occur
It proves the transient was shorter than one full logging interval
It can be interpolated to a 60 s interval to recover the transient
checks.explanation: The sampling interval sets a floor on resolution, so a 300 s interval neither captures nor disproves a 2 minute event. Claiming the transient did not occur treats absence of a low sample as evidence, which the interval geometry does not support.

checks.prompt: Logger memory wrapped and 40 minutes inside the event window is blank. How should that interval be entered in the event file?
choices: As a pressure excursion of unknown magnitude here
As normal pressure, since no low value was logged
As no data, with the interval flagged unresolved
As the average of the samples before and after it
checks.explanation: A gap is not a period of normal pressure and it is not evidence of an excursion either. The honest entry is no data with the interval marked unresolved; recording it as normal invents data the logger never captured.

checks.prompt: A crew collected a sample at 09:40 and returned the main to service at 10:15 while the laboratory result was still pending. Which statement about the timeline is correct?
choices: A pending result may be treated as satisfactory once flushing is done
Sample collection time can stand as the authorization timestamp here
Result received and return to service may share a single timestamp entry
Sample collected, result received and authorization are distinct events
checks.explanation: Collapsing sample collected, result received and authorization to return to service is the most common reconstruction failure. A result pending is not a satisfactory result, so treating it as satisfactory after flushing misstates the record.

checks.prompt: Using 9.804 kPa per metre of head, roughly how much pressure does a 9.8 m elevation rise account for between a hydrant gauge and an uphill service?
choices: About 96 kPa of added head loss uphill
About 9.8 kPa of added head loss uphill
About 48 kPa of added head loss uphill
About 960 kPa of added head loss uphill
checks.explanation: 9.8 m multiplied by 9.804 kPa/m is about 96 kPa. Reporting 9.8 kPa confuses metres of head with kilopascals, an error that understates the elevation effect by about a factor of ten at the point that matters.

checks.prompt: What is the correct status of the US EPA resource Drinking Water Distribution System Tools and Resources when cited in an Ontario integrity-event file?
choices: An Ontario requirement referenced by the disinfection procedure
United States technical guidance, not an Ontario requirement
A legal substitute for the facility operating procedures on site
A binding standard once it is cited in an Ontario event file
